(1 ch.) long in a straight line or '''chord''' between two points on the periphery of a curve,and then measuring the maximum distance of the rail from the '''chord''' at the centre of the 66 ft. The sense “sparkling wine” is believed to originate from an anecdote in 19th-century Berlin. The actor Ludwig Devrient supposedly ordered a bottle of wine using the phrase “from German Bring er mir Sekt,Schurke!”,based on the German translation of the line “Give me a cup of sack,(English),rogue!” from Shakespeare’s ''Henry IV''. *selbst*de{}|Etymology}With excrescent ''-t'' (same:eins > einst,su(n)s > sonst etc.) fossilized from the nonfeminine genitive singular from Middle High German sëlbes,from the from Old High German - pronoun from Old High German selb,from Old High German selbo,from Proto-Germanic ⋆selbaz,from Proto-Indo-European one's own,from Proto-Indo-European separate,apart. Compare from Low German sulv,from Dutch zelf,from English self,from Danish selv.|Pronunciation}IPA:/zɛlpst/official standard}IPA:/zɛlps/usually before a consonant; colloquially also in pausa}Ⓓ1/1f/De-selbst.ogg|Particle}selbst:}#personally,by oneself}•synononym selber}•Du hast es '''selbst''' zugegeben.}•You '''yourself''' admitted it.}•Der Mann '''selbst''' hat uns es gesagt.}•The man '''himself (personally)''' told us.|Derived terms}4}de}selb}selber}selber/selbe}selbig}selbstständig|Adverb}#even}•synononym sogar}•'''Selbst''' du hast es zugegeben.}•'''Even''' you admitted it.|Usage notes}DWDS labels selbst an indeclinable pronoun when it means “personally”,and an adverb when it means “even”. DWB labels it a pronoun when it means “personally”. The Duden labels it a particle in both senses.}selbst is generally understood to refer to the subject of the clause,whatever its position. Thus ''ich habe Sandra selbst gefragt'' means “I myself asked Sandra”,and not “I asked Sandra herself”. This can only be changed by placing the object at the beginning of the clause:''Sandra selbst habe ich gefragt'' (“Sandra herself was the one I asked”).

The class of the proletariat feels annihilated in estrangement; it sees in it its own powerlessness and the reality of an inhuman existence.

Was ist vornehm,267}#}:Es gibt ein Sprichwort bei den Chinesen,das die Mütter schon ihre Kinder lehren:siao-sin »mache dein Herz klein!« Dies ist der eigentliche Grundhang in späten Zivilisationen:ich zweifle nicht,daß ein antiker Grieche auch an uns Europäern von heute zuerst die '''Selbstverkleinerung''' herauserkennen würde – damit allein schon gingen wir ihm »wider den Geschmack«.+The Chinese have a proverb which mothers even teach their children:"Siao-sin" ("make thy heart small"). *Selbstverzwergung*de{}|Etymology}[selbst]+[Verzwergung]|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈzɛlpstfɛɐ̯ˌt͡svɛɐ̯ɡʊŋ/}Ⓓ8/87/De-Selbstverzwergung.ogg}Selbst+ver+zwer+gung|Noun}(fem.)}#self-dwarfing}•synononym Selbstverkleinerung}•Antonym:Größenwahn}#}'''2005''',Rainer-Mathias Limmer,''http://edoc.ub.uni-muenchen.de/3540/1/Limmer_Rainer_M.pdf Der Begriff der Anerkennung. Philosophisch-psychologische Untersuchungen'',Inaugural-Dissertation,LMU München,p.154}#}:Die halluzinierte Grenze des »Selbst« liegt am Anfang-Ende des »Vater- oder Mutterlandes«. Das Ich scheint so derartig instabil,»verletzlich«,dass es seine Grenzen ins vollkommen Imaginäre ausdehnen muss,damit sie mit der Grenze des Phanatasmas eine (un)gewisse Festigkeit erlangen,aber dort ins Rigide überschlagen. Der '''Selbstverzwergung''' entspricht der Größenwahn.

*sexy*de{}|Etymology}from Proto-Indo-European ⋆sek-}Borrowed en.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈzɛksi/qualifier:official standard but rarely used; usually considered overly formal or incorrect}IPA:/ˈsɛksi/qualifier:usual}Ⓓe/e2/De-sexy.ogg|Adjective}#sexy|Usage notes}In German,most people try to approximate the original pronunciations of many recently borrowed words,which is why there is even a term for this,Fremdwort,for which there is no real equivalent in English. In the case of the corresponding noun,''Sex'',a voiced beginning is considered even more outdated or incorrect than for the adjective ''sexy'',and this voiced pronunciation is used and emphasized for sechs ("six") to clearly differentiate it.}The positive form is not inflected in standard usage:''ein sexy Kleid''. Inflected forms only occur in colloquial speech (''ein sexyes Kleid''),and only rarely.}The comparative has to be inflected when used before nouns. This is avoided in standard usage,which means that the comparative is rare except in predicative position. (Colloquial:''Sie will ein sexyeres Kleid.''/''Sie will ein Kleid,das mehr sexy ist.'' Formal written:''Die Kundin sucht ein Kleid,das sexyer ist.'' Formal spoken since the ending of ''sexyer'' is hard to hear:''Die Kundin sucht ein Kleid,das mehr sexy ist.'')|Derived terms}unsexy

*sich*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German sich,from Old High German sih,from Proto-Germanic ⋆sek. Compare from Yiddish זיך,from Dutch zich.}This pronoun was originally restricted to the accusative case,while simple personal pronouns were used in the dative. Dative use of from Middle High German sich in from Middle High German - was restricted to northern dialects of Central German. In Early Modern German,a rare dative sir also occurred,formed by analogy with mir,dir. An obstacle to the generalisation of this form was the use of  in the plural,where there operated the conflicting analogy with the merged accusative/dative forms uns,euch.|Pronunciation}IPA:/zɪç/}Ⓓe/ea/De-sich.ogg}Ⓓ0/08/De-sich2.ogg}Rhymes:ɪç|Pronoun}sich:}#reflexive pronoun Reflexive pronoun of the third person singular:herself,himself,themself,itself,oneself (''direct'' or ''indirect object'')}#reflexive pronoun Reflexive pronoun of the third person plural:themselves (''direct'' or ''indirect object'')

*Sie*de{}|Alternative forms}-se|Etymology}rfe:de|Pronunciation}IPA:/ziː/}Ⓓ7/72/De-Sie.ogg}sie}Rhymes:iː|Pronoun}Sie:}#you polite; singular and plural}•Was möchten '''Sie''',Frau Wagner?}•What would '''you''' like to have,Mrs. Wagner?|Usage notes}The German ''Sie'' expresses distance in the relation between two persons. It is not perfectly correct to say that it expresses respect.  has never been used to address gods and saints. Towards parents it was only briefly used during the 18th century by some of the upper classes. (In both of these cases,however,Ihr was formerly possible alongside du.) Even royal highnesses used to be addressed as ''du'',albeit not personally but in songs and poems (compare the famous "w:Heil dir im Siegerkranz").}''Sie'' is identical in form to the third person plural pronoun sie and takes the same verb form. The "polite" ''Sie'' is distinguished in writing by capitalization. The only form which is not capitalized is the reflexive sich. When addressing a person with ''Sie'',one generally needs to replace the third person plural pronoun with the demonstrative die ("those ones") to avoid confusion:''Wissen Sie,was '''die''' zu mir gesagt haben?'' − “Do you know what they said to me?”|Derived terms}siezen|Anagrams}Eis}Pennsylvania German|Etymology}Compare from German Sie.|Pronunciation}IPA:/siː/|Pronoun}Sie:}#you qualifier:polite

This reflects a similar development for es/das.}While the genitive of personal pronouns does express ownership,it must not be confused with possessive pronouns. While possessive pronouns such as ihr are put in front of the noun they relate to and follow the inflection rules of adjectives,the genitive form of a personal pronoun has only one form,which is not further inflected. *sien*de{}|Pronunciation}IPA:/ziːn/|Pronoun}sien:}#Form of [sier]}Low German|Alternative forms}seyn,syn}sön Low Prussian|Etymology}From Middle Low German sîn,from Old Saxon sīn. The infinitive  along with the words is and sünd derive ultimately from Proto-Indo-European to be,which had no separate infinitive in Germanic. The modern infinitive was probably back-formed in late Old Saxon from the former first-person plural subjunctive from Old Saxon we be,since this form had become identical to the infinitive in other verbs during the late Old Saxon period. Compare also from German sein,from Dutch zijn.}The original infinitive is wesen,from Middle Low German wesen,from Old Saxon wesan,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆wesan,from Proto-Germanic ⋆wesaną,from Proto-Indo-European to reside. All the forms with initial ''w-'' (imperative and past tense) derive from this root. The infinitive wesen is still the most used one,but in general which one is used is a matter of personal preference and/or region.}Finally,the forms bün and büst derive from Proto-Germanic to be,to become,from Proto-Indo-European to become,which survives only as relic forms in the West Germanic languages and not at all in the others. Its infinitive and non-singular forms are only attested in (Old) English.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ziːn/|Verb}sien:(''past singular'' '''weer''',''past participle'' '''wesen''' or ''west'',''auxiliary verb'' '''wesen''')}#only as the infinitive wesen|Synonyms}wesen|See also}wesen

*Sinn machen*de{}|Etymology}Recorded in earlier rare use by Goethe,Lessing,Luther,and others,including "''Petrus der maister Lampardus,der die '''sentencias machet''',das ist das puch von hochen synnen zu teutsch''." From Medieval Latin (scholasticism) "from Latin sententiam facere".}has seen increasingly widespread use since the 1970s,probably due to the influence of the English expression make sense. Thus,the German expression is probably an interesting example of a rare case of a combination of a resurrected phrase and a modern loan translation. *Sitz im Leben*de{}|Etymology}Coined by Hermann Gunkel in 1930. lit:seat in life.|Noun}Sitz<m.sg> im Leben)}#idiomatic sociological setting|Usage notes}Though sometimes rendered by phrases like "life setting","situation in life" etc. the German term ''Sitz im Leben'' is better translated by "sociological setting" or left untranslated. As a technical term,it refers to the social setting of a text,particularly in the Bible. It is primarily used today in academic contexts,especially theology and biblical studies.

(Augsburger Bekenntnis)|Synonyms}wo}der}welcher|Interjection}so:}#colloquial a discourse marker in the beginning of a sentence indicating a topic having been deal with+dealt with and another being tackled}•synononym [[[[tamam],[okay]],[in Ordnung]],[fein]],[gut]}#}so '''So''',das sind die Entscheidungen der größten Gelehrten über die doch nicht ganz unwichtige Frage,wie eine der Sprachen auszusprechen sei,in der jahraus jahrein in Deutschland gutgezählte 50 000 junge Menschenkinder unterrichtet werden.Trotz jenen Entscheidungen ist natürlich noch lange nicht daran zu denken,daß dem Unfug einer als gänzlich falsch erkannten Aussprache des Griechischen ein Ende gesetzt wäre. Der Schlendrian wird auf diesem Gebiete des Schulwesens wohl ebenso lange dauern,wie auf vielen andern; denn bequem ist allerdings jener Schlendrian,nur wissenschaftlich ist er nicht,und unbrauchbar für das Leben ist er obendrein. Die Beseitigung des Schlendrians werde ich wohl nicht mehr erleben,auch dann nicht,wenn Plato selber aus der Asche auferstünde und die deutschen Schulmänner die richtige Aussprache lehrte. Sie würden ihm beweisen,daß er sich irre:er habe in den mehr als zwei Jahrtausenden seit seinem Tode gewiß die richtige Aussprache vergessen; sie aber,die deutschen Oberlehrer und Direktoren,kennten sie ganz genau:sie wäre buchstäblich so wie das Neuhochdeutsche des 20. Jahrhunderts gewesen.}•So these are the reckonings of the greatest scholars about the not quite insignificant question how one of the languages which is taught to about 50 000 young lads per annum should be pronounced.In spite of these reckonings by far it is not to think that this buffoonery of an utterly wrong pronunciation of Greek would come to an end. The litherness in this field of schooling will last as long as in many others; for convenient it is forsooth,but scientific it is not,and devoid of use for life ’tis on top. The elimination of this litherness I will not be an observer of in my lifetime,even if Plato himself were to rise from his ashes and teach the pedants the right pronunciation. They would shew him his being at fault:he surely has forgot the right pronunciation; but them,the senior and head teachers know it very well; it would be literally like the New High German of the 20th century.

When it is followed by ein,it's left undeclined.}:ein '''solches''' Auto.}•'''such''' a car}:'''solch''' ein Auto.}•'''such''' a car}If followed by an adjective,the word can be left undeclined. The following adjective is then declined strongly (as if without an article). *sollen*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German scholn,from Middle High German schuln,from Old High German sculan,from Old High German skulan,from Old High German scolan,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆skulan.}Cognate with from English shall and from English should,from Dutch zullen,from Danish skulle,from Swedish  and from Swedish skulle.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈzɔlən/}De-sollen.ogg(Germany)}De-at-sollen.ogg(Austria)|Verb}sollen(pretpres.soll#sollte,gesollt)}#auxiliary should; to be obligated (to do something); ought; shall}•Ich '''soll''' das machen.}•I '''should''' do that.}•Ich '''sollte''' das nicht tun.}•I '''should''' not do it.}#auxiliary to be recommended (to do something); to be asked (to do something)}#auxiliary to be intended (to do something); to be meant (to be something)}#auxiliary to be said (to do something); reportedly; they say that; I hear that; so they say; rumor has it; supposedly.}•Es '''soll''' da viele Leute geben.}•They say that there are many people there.}#auxiliary would; indicates that the subordinate clause indicates something that would happen in the past but after the time frame of the main clause}#auxiliary should; indicates that the subordinate clause indicates a hypothetical and unlikely condition for the main clause|Usage notes}''Sollen'' expresses moral duty or the suggestion that something ought to be done. müssen can express the necessity of doing something,but also the moral duty. Both verbs can express a duty imposed by someone else. In this case ''müssen'' is stronger than ''sollen'',implying that the imposing person has some kind of power to make the other really do it.}The following infinitive can be dropped if the meaning is clear from the situation. This is especially true with ''tun''.}Was soll ich heute?}•What should I do today?

*somatoform*de{}|Pronunciation}IPA:zomatoˈfɔɐ̯m}inline1|Adjective}#somatoform,(English)}#}somatoform Insbesondere bei Patienten mit '''somatoformen''' Störungen,denen bezüglich der psychogenen Erkrankungsanteile häufig die Störungseinsicht fehlt,gewinnt der Aspekt der Förderung der Behandlungsmotivation eminente Bedeutung (Baumeister u. *somatogen*de{}|Pronunciation}IPA:/zomatoˈɡeːn/}inline1|Adjective}#somatogenic}#}somatogen Gerade Patienten mit chronischen körperlichen Erkrankungen weisen häufig ein '''somatogen''' orientiertes Krankheitskonzept auf. Entsprechend ist ihre Behandlungserwartung oftmals passiv und eher an medikamentöser Therapie orientiert (Bengel et al. 2007). Folglich können Patienten mit chronischen somatischen Erkrankungen und komorbiden psychischen Störungen bisweilen nur schwer zur Teilnahme und Mitarbeit an psychologischen Angeboten oder an einer Psychotherapie motiviert werden.

*Sonnabend*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German sunābent,from Middle High German sunnenābent,from Old High German litSunday eve (9th c.),calqued on from Old English sunnanǣfen. In the Germanic reckoning,the day begins at sunset.}Compare from Low German Sünnavend,from West Frisian snjoen,from West Frisian sneaun,from West Frisian sneon.|Pronunciation}IPA:aastandard}IPA:aacolloquial}Ⓓd/d8/De-Sonnabend.ogg|Noun}(mask.,plural:[Sonnabendses])}#northern Germany Saturday}•synononym Samstag}#}Sonnabend Ist an einem bestimmten Tage oder innerhalb einer Frist eine Willenserklärung abzugeben oder eine Leistung zu bewirken und fällt der bestimmte Tag oder der letzte Tag der Frist auf einen Sonntag,einen am Erklärungs- oder Leistungsort staatlich anerkannten allgemeinen Feiertag oder einen Sonnabend,so tritt an die Stelle eines solchen Tages der nächste Werktag.:year1896:trans-titleCivil Code:chapter§ 193 Sonn- und Feiertag; Sonnabend:chapterurlhttps://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/bgb/__193.html:trans-chapterSundays and holidays; Saturdays:genre:translationIf a declaration of will has to be given or a service has to be rendered on a certain date,or within a period of time,and if said date,or the last day of said period,falls on a Sunday,on a holiday officially recognised at the relevant location or on a Saturday,then this day shall be replaced by the next workday.|Usage notes}''Sonnabend'' is still commonly used by older generations in northern Germany,whereas most younger people have adopted the southern/western Samstag. Since ''Sonnabend'' was the day's only official name in the German Democratic Republic,the word still enjoys a stronger position in eastern Germany,although the dominant ''Samstag'' is also gaining ground among the young.}Outside of these areas,might be used in the context of Roman Catholic masses held on Saturday evening,in order to emphasise that such masses count for fulfilling Sunday obligation. This is rare,however.|Derived terms}Sonnabendabend}sonnabendlich}Sonnabendmittag}Sonnabendmesse}Sonnabendmorgen}Sonnabendprediger}sonnabends}Sonnabendvormittag|See also}list:days of the week/de

*Sonntagsspaziergang*de{}|Etymology}From Sonntag (Sunday)+-s-+Spaziergang (walk) .|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈzɔntaːksʃpaˌt͡siːɐ̯ɡaŋ/}Ⓓb/b0/De-Sonntagsspaziergang.ogg|Noun}(mask.,genitive:Sonntagsspazierganges,plural:[Sonntägsspäziergänge])}#A recreational walk on a Sunday.}•sonntäglicher Spaziergang}#}quote-web:accessdate   2022-12-08}#by extension A relaxing walk on any day.}#}quote-web:accessdate   2022-12-08|Usage notes}''Sonntagsspaziergang'' usually means a walk on a Sunday.}In Germany/Austria/Switzerland,most people have the fewest obligations on a Sunday (no work,no school).}If the speaker is not talking about any particular Sunday,it could mean ''a relaxing walk on any day'' both the speaker and recipient are the least busy.}This includes Sunday,but could mean upcoming statutory holidays and possibly Saturdays,too.}Once a date for ''a relaxing walk on any day'' has been picked,it is usually not referred to as ''Sonntagsspaziergang'' anymore (except if it is indeed on a Sunday).|Hypernyms}Spaziergang

*Spekulatius*de{}|Etymology}unk:de. Various theories have been proposed:}Latinized form of Low German (especially East Frisian) ''Spikelātsje'',''Spekelātsje'' and Rhinelandic ''Spekulaties'' (19th c.),from  cog:speculatie meaning "plastically formed goodies" and later referred to "figured biscuits". One possible explanation for the Latinization of the Low German and Rhinelandic forms is that they were believed to be derived from m+:mirror,image,so that Latinization of these forms could take place.}From m+:spy,scout,which gave rise to the word ''Speculator'',which was the byname of Saint Nicholas. The reference to spying,scouting is comparable to Saint Nicholas' act of looking into the windows of poor families to help them out.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ʃpekuˈlaːt͡si̯ʊs/}Ⓓf/f4/De-Spekulatius.ogg|Noun}(mask.,genitive:Spekulatius,plural:[Spekulatius])}#speculoos

*ß*de{}|Alternative forms}de-CH-alt}rare|Pronunciation}s:phoneme IPA:/s/}s:letter name IPA:/ɛsˈtsɛt/Eszett,usual}s:letter name IPA:/ˈʃarfəs ˈɛs/scharfes S,less desirable because it also refers to the sound IPAchar:/s/regardless of its spelling|Letter}ß:}#Eszett or scharfes S,a German letter based on a ligature of '''ſ''' (long s) and '''z'''.|Usage notes}In alphabetic ordering,'''ß''' is equivalent to the string '''ss'''. For example,one would order:Maske,Maß,Masse,Maße,Massen,Maßen,Mast. The letter also alternates with '''ss''' in inflections and derivatives,e.g. lassen → past tense ließ,though such cases are now fairly rare.}The current rules for the choice between '''ß''' and '''ss''' were introduced in 1996. They follow the simple principle that '''ss''' is used after short vowels and '''ß''' otherwise (i.e. after long vowels and diphthongs). Hence  IPAchar:/ˈmasə/is distinguished from  IPAchar:/ˈmaːsə/. The earlier rules were more complicated and less phonetic. They prescribed that '''ß''' was additionally used in the syllable coda regardless of vowel length. Thus küssen,but ,and Faß,but Fässer (modern spelling küsst,Fass). The older spelling has become rare,but is still used by some older language users.}In Switzerland and Liechtenstein,the letter '''ß''' is not used at all. So Straße is spelt Strasse,and the above distinction between  and  is lost in favour of the latter. This use is also often seen in Luxembourg and occasionally in South Tyrol,but '''ß''' is standard in both of these areas. Moreover one encounters the same spelling in German books printed in w:antiqua script until the early 20th century,because an antiqua '''ß''' did not yet exist. A rarer alternative was to replace '''ß''' with '''sz'''.}It is standard to replace '''ß''' with '''SS''' in all caps:. However,in 2017 a new uppercase '''ẞ''' was introduced,so it is now also correct to spell . The use of a lowercase '''ß''' () is sometimes seen,but is proscribed. In capitalizing a few words which would become ambiguous if '''ß''' were changed to '''SS''','''SZ''' may be used instead,hence ''MASZE'' (''Maße'') may be kept distinct from ''MASSE'' (''Masse''),''BUSZE'' (''Buße'') from ''BUSSE'' (''Busse'').|Synonyms}Buckel-S}Doppel-S}Dreierles-S}Eszett}Ringel-S}Rucksack-S}scharfes S}Straßen-S

*ss*de{}|Symbol}ss:}#Sometimes used to replace the letter ß,especially when this key or character is not available. It was also the only official way of writing a capital '''ß''',until '''ẞ''' was officially adopted by the Council for German Orthography in June 2017.}#fromSLDE|Usage notes}In alphabetic ordering,the letter '''ß''' is equivalent to the string '''ss''' (formerly '''sz'''),so aß is sorted between Aspirin and Ast,immediately after the alphabetically equivalent Ass. The letter is never used in Swiss or Liechtenstein German,where it is always replaced by ss. Furthermore,ß was unique among the letters of the Latin alphabet as there was no capital form until ẞ was adopted in June 2017; in all-caps,all instances of ß were officially replaced by '''SS'''. However,not every instance of SS can be substituted back into ß.}Since the orthography reform from 1996,the letter ß is used only after long vowels and diphthongs. Before 1996,ß could also occur after short vowels at the end of a word or before a consonant. A rather large number of words that used to be spelled with ß ia now spelled with ss (for example,daß has become dass).|Synonyms}ß}Eszett}sz

*staunen*de{}|Etymology}Attested since the 17th century,then introduced in the general written language by Albrecht von Haller (1708-1777),from gsw,of uncertain origin. Probably related to stauen. Alternatively—though less likely both on semantic and phonetic grounds—from Old French estoner,whence from English astound,from English astonish. Probably not related to from English stun (from German stöhnen).}The original sense is “to become stiff,stand still”,used especially of the eyes and thus “to muse,contemplate,romanticise” (from German sinnen,schwärmen,schwelgen),which is the sense in which Haller used it. Compare english stood. Their a-vocalism is due to analogy with other strong verbs such as binden (''band'') and finden (''fand''),dating back to Middle-High German. This phrase originates from the Bible translation made by Martin Luther,<ref name"Pfeifer">{{R:DWDS</ref> in particular from the passage of Isaiah 8:14<ref name"Duden">Stein</ref> in which a trʾævæn næḡæf is mentioned in the original from Hebrew - version.|Pronunciation}IPA:ˌʃtaɪ̯n dɛs ˈʔanˌʃtoːsəs}Ⓓb/b7/De-Stein_des_Ansto%C3%9Fes.ogg}De-Stein des Anstoßes.oga}Stein des An+sto+ßes|Phrase}Stein des Anstoßes:}#idiom a source of annoyance}#}Stein des Anstoßes '''Stein des Anstoßes''' sind die folgenden Zeilen:„Vater unser im Himmel/Geheiligt werde die Lüge/Mein Fleisch verkomme/Mein Wille geschehe/Und den Himmel gib uns auf Erden/Und vergib uns unsere Gier/Drum führe uns jetzt in Versuchung/Und dann erlöse uns von all dem Bösen/Ich geb euch Liebe/Ich geb euch Hoffnung/Doch nur zum Schein/Denn die Massen woll’n betrogen sein.“:translationThe '''source of annoyance''' are the following lines:“Our Father in heaven/Hallowed be the lie/My flesh go rotten/My will be done/And give us heaven on earth/And forgive us our greed/So lead us now into temptation/And then deliver us from all evil/I give you love/I give you hope/Yet only in pretense/Because the masses want to be deceived.”}#}Stein des Anstoßes Zumindest die Vorbehalte gegenüber den Ultraorthodoxen scheinen die Kibbuzniks mit der weiteren Gesellschaft zu teilen. Besonders die Unterstützungsleistungen,die jene beziehen,bildeten an den Protesten in Tel Aviv einen zusätzlichen '''Stein des Anstoßes'''.:translationThe kibbutzniks seem to share at least the reservations about the ultra-Orthodox with the broader society. Especially the benefits that those receive created an additional '''source of annoyance''' at the protests in Tel Aviv.

*stochen*de{}|Etymology}Attested since the 16th century. In the 15th already the derivative . This ''gk''-spelling as well the late attestations suggest an adapted borrowing from gml,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆stokōn,whence from Dutch stoken,from English stoke. However,from Central Franconian - dialects show descendants of this which appear to be native (compare from Luxembourgish stachen),so it is also possible that the verb was inherited in northern Central German through from Middle High German ⋆stochen and later reinforced by Low German. The simplex did not establish itself in written German,but the frequentative stochern did.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈʃtɔxən/}Ⓓc/c6/De-stochen.ogg|Verb}de-verb}#rare to stoke,stir (fire)}•synononym [anfachen],[schüren]}#}stochen :de:year1941:chapterLehm:editorJosef Müller:titlew:langde:Rheinisches Wörterbuch|locationBonn|urlhttps://woerterbuchnetz.de/?sigleRhWB&lemidL02612|notecontaining the gerund  from ,italics in original|passageFrüher verwandte man im Ripuarischen,Nfrk Niederfränkischen (noch in Aachen,SNfrk Südniederfränkisch) zum Feuer'''stochen''' ''dat Gedecks'',das aus Kohlenstaub (''Gris'') u. Lehm,mit Wasser angemengt,besteht.|Derived terms}Stocher}stochern

*Storch*de{}|Alternative forms}Stork|Etymology}From Middle High German storch,from Middle High German storc,from Old High German storah,from Old High German ⋆storc(h),from Proto-West Germanic ⋆stork,from Proto-Germanic ⋆sturkaz.}Cognate to dialectal from Dutch stork,from English stork,from Swedish stork. The expected German form is also Stork,which was indeed in wide use,but has not become standardized. The shifted variant  is probably due to the use of epenthetic vowels in Old High German,by which the uninflected stem from Old High German storah alternated with inflected from Old High German storc-. Such variation was generally levelled in favour of the inflected stem,but this was an apparent exception. Compare for the regular development from Old High German starah alongside from Old High German starc(h),whence from Middle High German starc and modern stark. Alternatively,could be an Upper German relict form (with rx from rkx),but the regional distribution does not seem to confirm this.|Pronunciation}IPA:ʃtɔːç}Ⓓc/c0/De-Storch.ogg|Noun}(mask.,genitive:Storches,plural:[Storche],diminituve:Storch)}#stork gloss:bird|Derived terms}col-auto:Weißstorch

It is the only common preposition when referring specifically to the space between the houses (pavement and carriageway): When a street is used as a geographical location,however,in is more common:  In the latter example,which refers to a house,an is possible as a third alternative.|Synonyms}Str. abbreviation|Hyponyms}Anliegerstraße}Anwohnerstraße}Ausfallstraße}Bergstraße}Bundesstraße}Dorfstraße}Durchgangsstraße}Einfallstraße}Einkaufstraße}Europastraße}Fußgängerstraße}Hauptstraße}Hauptdurchgangsstraße}Hauptverkehrsstraße}Kantonalstraße}Kreisstraße}Landstraße}Magellanstraße}Milchstraße}Nebenstraße}Ortsstraße}Parallelstraße}Prachtstraße}Privatstraße}Querstraße}Sammelstraße}Schotterstraße}Seidenstraße}Seitenstraße}Verbindungsstraße}Wasserstraße}Wohnstraße}Zubringerstraße|Derived terms}Sträßchen,Sträßlein}straßenartig,straßenförmig}straßenlos

*Straßenbahn*de{}|Alternative forms}de-CH-alt|Etymology}From Straße.|Pronunciation}IPA:ˈʃtraːsənˌbaːn}Ⓓ2/24/De-Stra%C3%9Fenbahn.ogg|Noun}(fem.)}#streetcar,tramway}•synononym [[[[[[[[[Elektrische (dated)],[;]],[Tram (Austria]],[ Switzerland)]],[;]],[Trambahn]],[;]],[Tramway (Austria)]],[;]],[Straba (Saxony — Würzburg)]|Usage notes}An urban train might drive on the streets on paths that are also used by cars,or it might move in tracks separated from the rest of the road traffic in an open-air area called Gleiskörper,and it might drive underground in tunnels. It depends on the city whether the very same trains drive on all three tracks or whether there are different trains for the three types of tracks. In the latter case,as in Berlin,one w:distinguishes the three types by name,calling the one driving with the cars ''Straßenbahn'',the one on exclusive tracks S-Bahn,the ones serving the subway U-Bahn. Whereas in Cologne,(English) there is an indistinct Straßenbahn,U-Bahn or w:Stadtbahn,the w:S-Bahn being a means of transportation of greater distance to connect the whole urban area with its multiple cities. But in places where there isn’t such a tripartite system and a single train moves between tracks used by cars,exclusive s-train-tracks and tunnels in a single route,it is called Straßenbahn indistinctly,or also Stadtbahn,this last especially by the officials themselves,so in Bielefeld,the terms S-Bahn and U-Bahn being uncommon,the city being w:surrounded by rural areas otherwise only having busses for local traffic. Whereas in Hamburg “w:Straßenbahn” is a historical term since the Straßenbahnen proper have been abolished completely by 1978.|Descendants}only in Germany itself

*Streich*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German streich,from Old High German ⋆streih,from Proto-West Germanic tstroke. Compare from Dutch streek,from English stroke. In Middle High German the form from Middle High German strīch also occurs,which is either an adaptation to,or a new derivation from,the underlying verb streichen. In Modern Standard German both forms would have merged,but most dialects continue West Germanic ''ai''.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ʃtʁaɪ̯ç/}Ⓓ7/7a/De-Streich.ogg}Ⓓ2/22/De-Streich2.ogg}Rhymes:aɪ̯ç|Noun}(mask.,plural:[Streich(e)s])}#higher register stroke gloss:act of striking e.g. with a hand or a cutting weapon}•synononym [Hieb],[Schlag]}#figurative feat,coup gloss:quick and decisive act}•synononym [[Coup],[Schlag]],[Handstreich]}#by narrowing especially practical joke,prank|Derived terms}sense:stroke auf einen Streich,Backenstreich,Schwertstreich}sense:feat Staatsstreich}sense:prank Dumme-Jungen-Streich,einen Streich spielen
